第1-2题: A report published today by the Alderton Panel on Climate Finance concludes that spending on adaptation has risen for a third consecutive year, yet still covers less than a fifth of what the most exposed regions are estimated to need. The panel, made up of twelve economists and engineers, examined public budgets in forty-one countries. It found that money is increasingly directed towards sea walls and drainage systems, while far less is committed to early warning networks and to the retraining of farmers whose growing seasons have shifted. Dr. Nina Hale, who chaired the panel, said the imbalance was not accidental. Projects that produce a visible structure, she argued, are easier to announce and easier to audit than projects whose benefits depend on habits changing slowly over a decade. The report recommends that donors tie a fixed share of every adaptation grant to monitoring and to local training, and that progress be reviewed every two years rather than every five. Governments are expected to respond at a meeting in March.
第3-4题: Caldwell Library has completed a four-year project to photograph and publish its collection of medieval medical manuscripts, some of which have not been handled by anyone outside the library for more than a century. The collection consists of eighty-three volumes, many of them bound in covers that crumble at the hinge the moment they are opened. Rather than flattening the pages against a glass plate, the conservation team built a foam cradle for each volume, so that it could be photographed at an angle of no more than forty degrees. Every image was then checked by two readers working independently, because faded ink in the margins is easily mistaken for damage. The library has released the images without charge and without registration, a decision its director, Marcus Feld, described as a bet that use will justify the cost. Scholars have already begun to compare recipes for pain relief across the volumes, and a group in Veymouth reports that one instruction long dismissed as nonsense appears to describe a workable antiseptic.
第5-7题: A small biotechnology company has reported the results of a first-stage trial of a compound intended to slow the loss of muscle strength in patients with a rare inherited disorder. The trial enrolled thirty-six volunteers and lasted twelve weeks. Because the purpose of such a study is to establish safety rather than benefit, the primary measure was the number and severity of side effects; on that measure the compound performed acceptably, with headaches the most common complaint and no participant withdrawing. Secondary measures were more encouraging than the designers had expected. Patients who received the higher dose walked, on average, sixty metres further in six minutes than they had at the start, while those given the placebo changed hardly at all. The company's research director cautioned that the groups were small, that the trial had not been designed to compare doses, and that a twelve-week improvement may not persist. A second-stage trial, involving four hundred patients at eleven centres, is due to begin recruiting in the autumn.
第8-11题: Ellen: Tobias, have you read the latest message from the keynote speaker? Tobias: Only the first line. She has pulled out. Family reasons, apparently, and she suggests her deputy instead. Ellen: Her deputy. The one who wrote the book on harbour towns? Tobias: That is the one. I have read two of her chapters and they are sharp, but she is far less known. Half the registrations we have had so far probably came because of the original name. Ellen: Then we must decide this week, before the programme goes to press. If we announce the change now and explain why, people will accept it. If they discover it in April from the website, they will not. Tobias: Agreed. The other problem is the parallel sessions. We have nineteen papers and four slots, which means five papers in some rooms. Ellen: Five is too many. Twenty minutes each leaves no time for questions, and the questions are the reason people come. Tobias: We could shorten the papers to fifteen minutes and add a discussant to each session. That keeps the numbers and still leaves room for argument. Ellen: It also means finding eight discussants who will actually read the papers beforehand. Last time half of them arrived having skimmed the abstract. Tobias: We could pay them. Not much, but enough to make it a commitment rather than a favour. Ellen: Out of which budget? The travel grants are already stretched. Tobias: The publisher has offered to cover the printing of the abstract book. That frees about two thousand, and it is not a sum that would change anyone's travel plans. Ellen: All right. But I want the discussants named in the programme, so that if they do not deliver, it is visible. Tobias: Fair. And the poster session? Do we keep it on Thursday evening? Ellen: Move it to Friday lunchtime. People will actually walk past the posters if there is food.
第12-15题: Grace: So, Daniel, you said on the form that you are thinking of leaving the laboratory. What is pulling you away? Daniel: It is not the science. I like the science. It is that I spend six hours a day at a bench, and the part of the week I look forward to is explaining the work to visitors. Grace: Then let us take that seriously rather than treating it as a hobby. Have you written anything for a general audience? Daniel: A few pieces for the department newsletter. Nothing that anyone would call a portfolio. Grace: That is the first gap to close, and it is the cheapest one. Three or four short pieces, published somewhere with an editor who will cut them. The editing matters more than the publication. Daniel: I have been put off by the pay. Everyone I have spoken to says science writing pays badly at the start. Grace: It does, for the first two years. But you are comparing a starting salary with the salary you would reach in four years if you stayed. That comparison always looks bad, and it is the wrong one. Daniel: So what is the right one? Grace: Whether the ceiling is higher, and whether you can live on the floor for a while. Do you have savings? Daniel: About four months' worth. Grace: Then do not resign. Ask for a four-day week, use the fifth day for writing, and give yourself a year. If by next summer you have six published pieces and no income from them, you will know something. Daniel: And if I do have income? Grace: Then you negotiate from strength rather than from hope. One more thing: talk to people doing the job now, not to people who left it five years ago. The work has changed.
第16-18题: Universities routinely list critical thinking among their graduate aims, and just as routinely assume that it will appear once students have acquired enough subject knowledge. The assumption is convenient, because it requires no change to the timetable. It is also largely unsupported. Studies that follow students through a degree find that the ability to weigh evidence improves modestly at best, and that most of the improvement occurs in departments where argument is taught explicitly rather than absorbed by example. What explicit teaching looks like is less mysterious than the phrase suggests. In one design, students are given two accounts of the same event, written from opposing positions, and asked to list the claims that both accounts accept. The exercise is uncomfortable, because most students arrive expecting to choose a side. Its value lies in showing that disagreement usually rests on a narrow base of shared fact, and that identifying that base is a skill which can be practised. A second design asks students to write the strongest version of the argument they reject. This is harder still, and it exposes a common failure: students can often state an opposing view, but they state it in a form no reasonable person would hold, which makes refutation easy and learning impossible. None of this requires smaller classes or new technology. It requires that the reasoning be made visible, that students be asked to produce it under conditions they cannot avoid, and that someone with expertise mark the result. The obstacle is not money but the reluctance of departments to surrender time currently spent on content. Content, after all, is what examinations reward.
第19-21题: Most cities now regulate the noise of individual machines: a lorry, a drill, a ventilation unit must each stay below a stated limit. The approach has an obvious appeal, since a limit can be written into a permit and checked with a meter. It also fails to address the problem residents actually complain about, which is the sum of many sources that are each perfectly legal. A street may contain a dozen refrigeration units, each quiet enough to pass inspection, whose combined hum at three in the morning is what wakes the people living above the shop. No single owner is responsible, and no inspector has the authority to require that any one of them be switched off. Regulation designed around sources cannot see a total. The second difficulty is measurement. A reading taken at a bedroom window over ten minutes will miss the delivery that arrives at half past five, and it will also miss the fact that a sound tolerable in July, with windows open, is intolerable in January, when the same plant runs all night. Averaging over time produces numbers that are defensible in court and meaningless to the person who cannot sleep. Some cities have begun to regulate zones rather than machines, setting a ceiling for an area and then allocating it, much as a cap on emissions is allocated among firms. The advantage is that it makes the total visible and forces a decision about who must reduce. The disadvantage is political: allocating a scarce resource means telling someone that their share is smaller than they had assumed, and few councils relish that conversation before an election.
第22-25题: Arguments about artificial intelligence and employment tend to be conducted in totals: either machines will take most jobs, or they will take very few. Both claims are probably wrong, and both are unhelpful, because what matters is not the number of jobs but their shape. The pattern visible so far is not mass dismissal but the hollowing out of the middle. Tasks that can be described precisely enough to be automated tend to be the tasks of clerical and technical workers, whose jobs consist of applying known rules to known cases. The work that remains at the top involves judgement under uncertainty, and the work at the bottom involves physical presence in unpredictable settings. A firm that automates its claims processing does not usually close; it hires fewer clerks and more people who can supervise the system and explain its decisions to customers and regulators. The consequence is a change in the ladder rather than the disappearance of the building. Entry-level positions have traditionally been where people learned the judgement that the higher positions require. If the entry-level task is automated, the learning is removed along with it, and firms discover after several years that they have no internal candidates for roles they assumed would fill themselves. This is not an argument for preserving jobs that no longer need doing. It is an argument for rebuilding the bottom rung deliberately, through apprenticeships, through supervised projects, and through a willingness to employ people before they are fully productive. The cost of doing so is visible on a budget line; the cost of not doing so appears a decade later, in the form of a shortage that no salary seems able to fill.
